To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cubic and peanut-shaped microparticle monolayers at the oil-water interfaces of Pickering emulsifiers form solid-stabilised o/w emulsifiers via the process of coalescence.

cubic hematite microparticle monolayers at the oil-water interfaces form stable, long-lived emulsions and that the interfacial packing of cubes and peanuts is different from that of spherical particles.

cubic and peanut-shaped microparticle assemblies at the oil-water surface display a local packing density higher than theoretically achievable in a monolayer of spheres and that the particles preferentially orient at the interface.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of particle anisotropy on the stability of solid-stabilized emulsions.
the effect of anisotropic particles on the interfacial organization and stability of Pickering emulsifiers.
the effect of particle geometry on emulsion stability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the particle shape has an influence on the packing at the interface and on the orientation of particles at the interface.

the particle shape anisotropies of cubes and peanuts do not have any influence on the emulsion stability, but they do have an influence on the interfacial packing density and orientation of the particles.
the packing density of the anisotropic particles is higher than for spheres, whereas the interfacial orientation is more stable, which leads to a lower interfacial deformation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
particle shape anisotropies can be exploited for the design of novel, stable emulsions.
the interfacial packing density of anisotropic particles can be higher than that of spherical particles, and that the shape anisotropies can be used to tune the interfacial orientation of particles.
cubic and peanut-shaped microparticle monolayers are stable and form stable emulsions with a packing density of 90%, whereas spherical monolayers have a packing density of only 65%.
The main takeaway from our work is that
anisotropic micrometre-sized particles may be used to stabilize emulsions with a high degree of interfacial organization and that this is not only limited to the use of spheres or ellipsoids.
anisotropy of the microparticle shape can be exploited to achieve a high degree of control over the structure of the adsorbed particle monolayer and the resulting emulsion.
the shape of particles is an important parameter to control the interfacial packing density and orientation of particles at liquid-liquid interfaces.
